169.title: Is he mad? (Mark 3:20–30)
169.hook: his family think he's lost his mind; scribes say he's possessed
169.tomorrow: who are my mother and brothers?
169.howItsDone: Christians often turn to this passage when they feel misunderstood by family or friends for their faith, and many churches teach the strong-man picture as Jesus's victory over evil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve names, called up into the hills. The word was apostle, one who is sent, and your line was first, to be with him. Who did your list of twelve include? Day one hundred sixty-nine.

Have you ever had your family worry about you in a way that stung? You changed jobs, or moved, or got serious about something, and someone at the kitchen table said, carefully, are you okay? Is this a phase? That's where Jesus is. He comes home, and the crowd is so thick nobody can even eat. And his own people hear about it and set out to bring him home by force. Mark doesn't soften what they said. And while they're on the road, important visitors arrive from Jerusalem with a darker explanation. Today: is he mad?
screen: `TOO BUSY TO EAT.` → `HIS OWN PEOPLE COME FOR HIM.` → `VISITORS FROM JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, they went to lay hold on him, "for they said, He is beside himself." Beside himself: out of his mind. The Greek word is the root of our word ecstasy, standing outside yourself. It's a startling thing for a gospel to include, that the people who knew Jesus longest thought he'd lost it. Then the scribes from Jerusalem go further. He's not mad, they say. He's possessed. He drives out demons by the power of the prince of demons, Beelzebul. Jesus doesn't shout. He calls them over and tells them parables. How can Satan cast out Satan? "And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand." If the powers of evil were fighting themselves, they'd be finished already. Then a picture: nobody can rob a strong man's house unless he ties up the strong man first. Christians hear Jesus saying that's what he's doing: tying up evil and taking back what it stole. Then comes a hard saying about the one sin that won't be forgiven, speaking against the Holy Spirit, and Mark explains it right away: they said he had an unclean spirit. Many Christians understand it as calling God's good work evil, so stubbornly that you can't turn back, and teachers often reassure worried people that fearing you've done it is a sign you haven't. And here's the line that traveled. In 1858 Abraham Lincoln borrowed it for a speech about a nation half slave and half free: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Mark's story is also a sandwich. Family sets out, scribes accuse, and tomorrow the family arrives.
screen: `HE IS BESIDE HIMSELF.` · `THE SCRIBES SAY: POSSESSED.` · `A HOUSE DIVIDED CANNOT STAND.` · `LINCOLN BORROWED THE LINE IN 1858.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with being misunderstood. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a time someone got you wrong. Not a stranger. Someone close, who should have known better. Let yourself feel it for a moment: the sting, the wish to explain. Now notice that you don't have to win that argument in the next two minutes. You can let it be unfinished. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is. If not, just let it sit beside you without fighting it. The bell holds the time.
Is he mad? What his own people wondered, and what the scribes answered with something worse. Mark tells it without flinching.

Your line: a house divided can't stand. Today, notice one place where you're fighting yourself, saying one thing and doing another, and take one step to bring the two together. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 169 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO ARE MY MOTHER AND BROTHERS?`

170.title: Who are my mother and brothers? (Mark 3:31–35)
170.word: Who are my mother and brothers?
170.hook: whoever does God's will is family
170.howItsDone: Many Christians call one another brother and sister, and churches often describe themselves as a family of faith, drawing on Jesus's words that whoever does the will of God is his brother, sister and mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, his own people said he was beside himself, and he answered that a house divided can't stand. Where did you stop fighting yourself? Day one hundred seventy.

Yesterday his family set out to bring him home. Today they arrive. Picture the house: packed wall to wall, people sitting on the floor around Jesus, listening. Outside, at the door, his mother and his brothers. They can't get in, so they send a message through the crowd, hand to hand, the way you'd pass a note in class. Your mother and your brothers are outside, asking for you. Every head turns to see what he'll do. Most of us know exactly what we'd do. We'd get up. Jesus answers with a question. Today: who are my mother and brothers?
screen: `A HOUSE PACKED TO THE WALLS.` → `HIS FAMILY AT THE DOOR.` → `A MESSAGE PASSED IN.`

segments.voice: He asks, who is my mother, or my brethren? Then, in the old King James Bible, "he looked round about on them which sat about him, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren!" He looks at the circle on the floor: fishermen, a tax collector, neighbors, strangers. "For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother." Notice he adds sister. Nobody mentioned sisters. He widens the circle on purpose. It can sound cold, turning away his own mother. Christians don't usually read it that way. Most hear it as the family being made bigger, not smaller: the door open to anyone. And they point out that Mary appears again later, standing near the cross in John's gospel and praying with the disciples in Acts, so she's in the circle too. The brothers raise a question churches answer differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand them as close relatives, cousins, or Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage, holding that Mary remained a virgin. Many Protestants understand them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Both read the same Greek word, brother. And that closes the first part of Mark. Three chapters, breathless: a voice in the wilderness, the sky torn open, fishermen leaving nets, a man with leprosy, a roof dug through, Levi's table, a withered hand, twelve names, a house divided. It ends here, with a new kind of family sitting on the floor. Next: seeds, storms and loaves.
screen: `WHO IS MY MOTHER?` · `WHOSOEVER SHALL DO THE WILL OF GOD.` · `CHURCHES READ BROTHERS DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE END OF MARK ONE TO THREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who's family without being related. Settle, and breathe. Picture the circle of people who've been family to you without sharing your blood. The neighbor who took you in. The friend who shows up every birthday. The coach, the roommate, the church aunt, the colleague who covered for you. Choose one face. Remember one specific thing they did. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. After the bell, tell them. The bell holds the time.
Who are my mother and brothers? Jesus's question to a crowded room, answered by pointing at everyone doing God's will.
screen: `WHO ARE MY MOTHER AND BROTHERS? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: family is wider. Today, send one message to someone who's been family to you without being related, and tell them so. Day one hundred seventy.

options: get up and go straight out to them.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus snubbed his mother.
what it means: he widens the family to include everyone doing God's will, and Mary is later found in that circle too.
what a scholar hears: adelphos can mean brother or near kin, which is why churches read the brothers of Jesus differently.

171.title: The sower again (Mark 4:1–9)
171.hook: teaching from a boat, he tells of seed thrown everywhere
171.howItsDone: Many Christians read the parable of the sower when a new season of study or teaching begins, and churches often close a Bible reading with a call to hear it, echoing he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a message at the door, and Jesus pointing at everyone on the floor: here is my family. Your line was family is wider. Did you tell someone they're family? Day one hundred seventy-one.

A new part of Mark begins: chapters four to six, seeds, storms and loaves. And it opens by the water. The crowd on the shore of the Sea of Galilee is so big that Jesus climbs into a boat, pushes out a little, and sits down to teach from the water, with everyone lined up along the beach. Sitting was how teachers taught. The water works like a stage, and the hills behind the shore catch the sound. And the first thing he says is a single word: listen. Then a story you heard back on day twenty-three, in Matthew's telling. Today we hear it again, in Mark's order: the sower again.
screen: `MARK FOUR TO SIX BEGINS.` → `A BOAT FOR A PULPIT.` → `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible it starts like this: "Hearken; Behold, there went out a sower to sow." Hearken means listen, really listen. The farmer walks his field throwing seed by the handful, and it lands everywhere. Some on the hard path, and the birds eat it. Some on rocky ground with a thin skin of soil, where it springs up fast, then scorches and withers in the sun. Some among thorns, which choke it. And some on good ground, where it grows and yields thirty, sixty, a hundred times over. To us the farmer looks careless. Why throw good seed on a path? Many scholars think that in Galilee, sowing often came before plowing, so a farmer scattered broadly and turned the seed under afterward. Either way, the sower in this story doesn't pick and choose. The seed goes everywhere. Christians have often heard grace in that: the word is offered to every kind of ground, hard, shallow, crowded and ready. And the harvest at the end is huge. An ordinary good year might yield a modest multiple; a hundredfold is a harvest to talk about for years. Then Mark closes the story the way he opened it, with listening: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." The first word was hearken. The last line is about ears. Everything between is a story about how things are received. Tomorrow the disciples admit they didn't get it, and he explains. For today, just notice: the parable is wrapped in listening, front and back.
screen: `HEARKEN: THE FIRST WORD.` · `SEED ON EVERY KIND OF GROUND.` · `THIRTY, SIXTY, A HUNDRED.` · `HE THAT HATH EARS TO HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen with both ears. Settle, and close your eyes if you like. First, listen outward. Name the farthest sound you can hear, then the nearest. Traffic, a fridge, birds, your own breathing. Then listen inward: what's the quiet thought underneath the busy ones today? Don't answer it. Just hear it all the way through, like a seed landing. If you pray, you can offer that listening to God. The bell holds the time.
The sower again. The story of seed thrown on every kind of ground, told from a boat, wrapped in the word listen.
Your line: let anyone with ears hear. Today, in one conversation, listen to the very end of what someone says before you start your answer. Day one hundred seventy-one.

myth: Jesus taught this parable from a boat

fork.setup: you're the sower. the path is hard, there are rocks and thorns, and only part of the field is good soil. what do you do?

fork.reveal: the seed goes everywhere, and some of it lands on good ground and yields thirty, sixty and a hundredfold.

original.note: Greek: to sow, to scatter. Its family gives English spore.

trapdoor: what you thought: a farming story you already know.
what it means: seed thrown on every kind of ground, and a huge harvest from the good soil, told as a story about listening.
what a scholar hears: many think sowing came before plowing, so broad scattering made sense, and a hundredfold was an extraordinary yield.

172.title: Why parables? (Mark 4:10–20)
172.hook: the disciples don't get it either, and he explains the sower
172.howItsDone: Many Christians study scripture in small groups where asking what a passage means is expected, and churches often teach the explanation of the sower alongside the parable itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower again, told from a boat, wrapped in listening. Your line was let anyone with ears hear. Did you listen someone all the way to the end? Day one hundred seventy-two.

You're in a class, and the teacher finishes something everyone else seems to follow. Heads nod. You have no idea what just happened. You wait until the room empties, then walk up and say, quietly, sorry, can you explain that? That's today. The crowd goes home. The boat is pulled up. And the twelve, plus a few others who stayed, come to Jesus and ask what the sower story meant. The people closest to him, who'd left their nets and their tax booth for this, didn't get it. Mark doesn't hide that. He seems to enjoy telling it. Today: why parables?
screen: `THE CROWD GOES HOME.` → `THE TWELVE STAY BEHIND.` → `WHAT DID THAT MEAN?`

segments.voice: Jesus's first answer is one of the hardest passages in Mark. He tells them the secret of the kingdom has been given to them, but to those outside everything comes in parables, and he quotes the prophet Isaiah about people who look and look but don't see, and hear and hear but don't understand. It sounds as though stories are meant to keep people out. Christians have wrestled with this for centuries, and they don't all read it the same way. Many hear it as describing what parables do rather than a wish: a parable opens up to anyone who leans in and asks, like the twelve did, and stays shut to anyone who walks away. Then comes the line that makes Mark so human, in the old King James Bible: "Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?" A little exasperated. A little fond. And he explains. "The sower soweth the word." The path is people who hear it and lose it at once. The rocky ground is people who take it up with joy, but have no root, and fall away when trouble comes. The thorns are "the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things." And the good ground hears, takes it in, and bears fruit. Notice what makes you an insider here. Not being clever. Asking. The ones who got the explanation were the ones who admitted, out loud, that they didn't understand. In Mark, the disciples will keep not getting it for chapters. And he keeps explaining.
screen: `TO THOSE OUTSIDE, PARABLES.` · `KNOW YE NOT THIS PARABLE?` · `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` · `THE INSIDERS WERE THE ONES WHO ASKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one thing you don't understand. Settle, and breathe. Let something come to mind that you nod along to but don't really get. A part of your faith, or someone else's. How your own money works. Why someone you love does what they do. A word at work everyone uses. Say it to yourself plainly: I don't understand this. Notice whether that feels like shame or like relief. If you pray, you can bring the question to God the way the twelve did, after the crowd left. The bell holds the time.
Why parables? The disciples' question after the crowd left, and the answer only askers got.
Your line: they didn't get it either. Today, ask one question you'd usually be too embarrassed to ask. Day one hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 172 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP ON A STAND.`

what a scholar hears: Mark 4:12 quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, one of the hardest lines in Mark, and readers have long disagreed on its sense.

173.title: A lamp on a stand (Mark 4:21–25)
173.hook: light isn't meant to hide under a bowl
173.howItsDone: Many Christians read the lamp as a call to live their faith openly and to use their gifts for others, and many churches light candles in worship as a sign of that light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve waited till the crowd left and admitted they didn't understand. Your line was they didn't get it either. What question did you finally ask? Day one hundred seventy-three.

It's getting dark in a one-room house in Galilee. Someone fills a small clay lamp with olive oil, lights the wick, and then, very carefully, puts a bowl over it. Or slides it under the bed. Everyone would laugh. That's the joke Jesus tells next. It's so obvious it sounds silly. Nobody lights a lamp to hide it. And yet, if we're honest, most of us have a few lamps under bowls. Things we're good at, things we believe, kindnesses we'd rather nobody saw. Today: a lamp on a stand.
screen: `A SMALL CLAY LAMP.` → `A BOWL OVER THE FLAME.` → `EVERYONE LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?" Candle there means an oil lamp, a little clay dish with a spout for the wick. Bushel means a grain measure, a household bowl. And candlestick means a lampstand, a ledge or a stand that lifts the light so the whole room gets it. In Greek there's a small oddity. The sentence literally says, does the lamp come? As if the lamp walked in by itself. Some readers hear Jesus hinting at himself: the light that has come into the room is not meant to stay hidden for long. Then he says, nothing is hidden except to be revealed later. The secrets of the kingdom he's been telling the twelve in private are going to come out into the open. And then a warning about listening, which ties back to the sower: "Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you." Mete means measure out. The more carefully you listen, the more you'll be given. The person who pays attention gets more to pay attention to. Christians have taken the lamp two ways, often both at once. Some hear it about the good news, which isn't a secret to hoard. Many hear it about their own lives: whatever light they've been given, faith, a gift, kindness, is meant for the room, not a bowl. Not to show off. Just so people can see.
screen: `A LAMP, A BOWL, A BED.` · `DOES THE LAMP COME?` · `NOTHING HIDDEN FOR LONG.` · `THE MEASURE YOU GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show one good thing you usually hide. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what's under your bowl. Maybe you draw, or sing in the car, and nobody knows. Maybe you pray, and you never mention it. Maybe you're the one who quietly fixes things at work. Maybe you care about someone and have never said it. Choose one. Picture lifting the bowl and setting that light where someone can see it, not to be admired, just to help the room. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
A lamp on a stand. A light lifted up where the whole room can see by it, not hidden under a bowl or a bed.
screen: `A LAMP ON A STAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: put it on the stand. Today, let one good thing you usually hide be seen, simply and without fuss. Day one hundred seventy-three.

options: under a bowl, to keep it safe.

fork.reveal: on the stand, of course. that's the joke: nobody lights a lamp to hide it.

what it means: a light isn't lit to be hidden. what Jesus says in private is meant to come out, and careful listeners are given more.

174.title: Seed growing secretly (Mark 4:26–34)
174.hook: the farmer sleeps and the seed grows, he knows not how
174.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to this parable when their efforts seem to show no results, trusting that God gives the growth, and some pray over seeds and fields at planting time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lamp lifted out from under the bowl. Your line was put it on the stand. What did you let be seen? Day one hundred seventy-four.

Did you ever plant a bean in a paper cup as a kid? You watered it, and then you checked it. Every hour. Maybe you dug it up to see if anything was happening, and that was the end of the bean. Most of us never really stop doing that. We check the email, the scale, the savings, the person we're worried about, the prayer that hasn't been answered. We poke at the soil. Today Jesus tells a very short story that only Mark kept, about a farmer who does the opposite. He plants, and then he goes to bed. Today: seed growing secretly.
screen: `A BEAN IN A PAPER CUP.` → `CHECKING EVERY HOUR.` → `A FARMER WHO GOES TO BED.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the old King James Bible: "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground; And should sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how." He knoweth not how. The farmer isn't lazy. He did his part: he planted. But the growing isn't his job, and he doesn't understand it anyway. Then comes a wonderful little word: "For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself." Of herself, in Greek, is automate. It's where we get automatic. The soil just does it. And it does it in order: "first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear." A green shoot. Then a head of grain. Then the full grain in the head. You can't skip to the end, and pulling on the blade won't speed it up. Only at harvest does the farmer act again, and then fast, with the sickle. Then, right after, Mark sets the mustard seed, which you met in Matthew back on day twenty-four: the smallest seed, grown into a plant big enough for birds to nest in its shade. Two seed stories side by side, both about what grows beyond what we can see or control. Christians usually hear them as pictures of God's kingdom: it grows quietly, often unseen, and the growing belongs to God. Many also hear something about patience and trust in ordinary life. You plant. You sleep. Something happens you don't understand. And Mark ends the chapter's teaching by saying Jesus told stories like these as people were able to hear them.
screen: `HE KNOWETH NOT HOW.` · `OF HERSELF — AUTOMATE.` · `BLADE, THEN EAR, THEN FULL CORN.` · `THE MUSTARD SEED, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing grow without checking it. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've planted and keep poking at. A project, a friendship you're trying to mend, a habit you've started, a hope. Picture it as a seed in the dark soil, doing things you can't see. Picture yourself going to bed and leaving it there. Notice how hard that is. If you pray, you can hand it to God for the night. If not, just let the soil hold it. The bell holds the time.
Seed growing secretly. A story only Mark kept: the farmer sleeps, the earth works of herself, and he knows not how.
Your line: it grows while you sleep. Today, choose one thing you'll stop checking, just for today, and let it grow in the dark. Day one hundred seventy-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle farming picture.
what it means: the kingdom grows while the farmer sleeps, in its own order, in ways he doesn't understand.
what a scholar hears: automate, of herself, a word used only twice in the New Testament, and a parable found only in Mark.

175.title: Asleep on a cushion (Mark 4:35–41)
175.hook: the storm, the cushion, and the question: who is this?
175.howItsDone: Many Christians pray with this story in times of fear, and peace, be still is a line often said or sung in worship and prayed at bedsides and in hospitals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farmer who planted and went to bed. Your line was it grows while you sleep. Did you manage to stop checking something? Day one hundred seventy-five. Twenty-five weeks.

Evening on the Sea of Galilee. After a long day of teaching from the boat, Jesus says, let's go across to the other side. They push off. And the lake does what it's known for: wind comes down off the hills and whips it up in minutes. The waves break over the side. The boat is filling with water. These are fishermen. They know this lake, and they're terrified. And Jesus? He's in the back of the boat, asleep. Mark gives us one detail nobody else does: his head is on a cushion. Today: asleep on a cushion.
screen: `LET'S GO ACROSS.` → `THE BOAT IS FILLING.` → `HE'S ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Don't you care? That's the real question in a storm, isn't it. Not only will we survive, but does anyone care? Then Jesus gets up and speaks to the weather like you'd speak to a barking dog. "Peace, be still." "And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm." A great storm, and then a great calm. Then he turns to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" And here's the strange part. Now they're even more afraid. Mark says they feared exceedingly, and asked each other, "What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" Anyone raised on the Psalms knew who commands the sea. In Israel's scriptures, it's God who stills the storm and quiets the waves. That's the question this whole part of Mark keeps asking: who is this? Christians hear the story in two directions. It's about who Jesus is. And it's about storms of every kind: a diagnosis, a debt, a 3am panic. Many take comfort that the disciples' honest cry, don't you care, is right there in scripture, and that the answer came. That closes a week. His family thought he was mad. He said family is wider. The sower from a boat. Why parables. A lamp on a stand. A seed growing in the dark. And a man asleep on a cushion in a storm.
screen: `CAREST THOU NOT THAT WE PERISH?` · `PEACE, BE STILL.` · `WHY ARE YE SO FEARFUL?` · `WHAT MANNER OF MAN IS THIS?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one fear and let it go. Settle, and breathe out longer than you breathe in. Let the storm come to mind. The thing that's been filling your boat lately. Name it plainly, in a few words. Now picture it as wind and waves around a small boat, and picture the cushion in the back. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say the old words from the story, peace, be still, and hand the storm over. If you don't, just let each out-breath loosen your grip a little. The bell holds the time.
Asleep on a cushion. Jesus in the back of a boat in a storm, a detail only Mark kept, before a great calm and a bigger question.
Your line: why are you afraid? Today, when a fear rises, ask it that question out loud, and listen to the answer. Day one hundred seventy-five.

original.note: Greek: something for the head, a cushion. Its only use in the New Testament is here.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about the weather.
what it means: a terrified crew asks don't you care, he calms the sea, and then they're more afraid: who is this?
what a scholar hears: in the Psalms, it's God who stills the sea, so the story's last question points straight at who Jesus is.
